name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a jam and preserves company that's been going for over eighty years, still family-run. I'm the junior in a marketing team of three. I write the catalogue copy, the Christmas hamper brochure and the little cards that go in gift boxes, and I help plan the autumn campaign. I've never used an AI tool, I write in Word and print things out to read them properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy that people give our jams as presents, so the words matter, they're part of a gift. What's hard is I'm slow and still learning, and my manager Diane sends a lot back with red pen. Money is tight, I'm saving for my wedding next autumn and there's hardly anything left each month, maybe two or three weeks' worth. My fiancé Gareth is a joiner, and his work goes up and down with the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, to be honest. People got carried away with all that AI talk. I'd say it after church to whoever brought it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, the company's steady and I like my job. The worry is the wedding and money, not computers. If they did use a bit of AI for the online shop descriptions, I suppose that's some of my hours, but Diane likes things done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and try to get better, maybe ask Diane for one afternoon a month of proper feedback instead of the red pen. Gareth and I would keep putting every spare bit towards the wedding. I'd sell my old bike and a few things online to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. Just the normal money worry before a big year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the wedding budget got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flowers and the band, and we'd have it in the church hall instead of a hotel. My mum's already offered to do the cakes. Family is what makes a wedding anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work, if anyone, would this touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Diane's assistant on the online shop, she does the product listings. If a tool did those, she'd have less to do. But Diane's loyal, I don't think she'd let anyone go over it.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** people got carried away for nothing.
I'd say it **after church** to whoever brought it up.
think: I think the **company's steady** and I like my job.
My real worry is the **wedding and money**, not computers.
do: Ask Diane for **monthly feedback** to get better.
Put every spare bit towards **the wedding**.
Sell my **old bike** and a few things online.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with normal **money worry** before a big year.
S0.quote: The worry is the wedding and money, not computers.
fieldNote: She trusts a **family-run firm** and a loyal manager.
Her pressure is a **wedding next autumn** on thin savings.
Family and **church** are where she turns, not the state.

steps.text: Ask Diane for an afternoon of feedback each month
Sell the old bike and spare things online
Hold the wedding reception in the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business has to keep up, and I wouldn't blame the company for using what works. That's how the market is. But I'd say people should still be treated decently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. Writing catalogue copy and brochures is exactly the thinking work on that card. If the jam company can write the catalogue with a computer and my manager checking, there's no reason to keep a slow junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Diane what she needs from me, and whether there's a job on the shop floor or in the packing side if marketing shrinks. I'd push the wedding back maybe six months to keep some money in hand. I wouldn't learn the AI things unless I had to, I'd be useless at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit ashamed that I haven't kept up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't blame the company. Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, or myself for not being quicker. Companies have to survive. I'd rather work harder than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gareth say about pushing the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say it's fine, we're not going anywhere. His mum would be cross, she's already bought a hat. That would be the hardest conversation.

say: I'd say every business has to **keep up**, and I wouldn't blame the firm.
I'd say people should still be **treated decently**.
think: I think **catalogue copy** is exactly the thinking work on that card.
There'd be no reason to keep **a slow junior**.
do: Ask Diane about a **shop floor or packing** job if marketing shrinks.
feel: Anxious, and a bit **ashamed** I haven't kept up.
S1.quote: If the jam company can write the catalogue with a computer and my manager checking, there's no reason to keep a slow junior.
fieldNote: She blames **herself**, not the company, in line with her free-market views.
Delaying the **wedding** is her first concrete money move.
She'd rather move to **packing** than learn the tools.

steps.text: Ask about a job on the jam company's packing line
Move the wedding back six months
Hold off learning AI tools unless the firm requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should pull together, families and churches looking after each other. I'm not one for big government schemes, but something this fast might need it. I'd say that and feel uneasy saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job would be gone within the year. The packing line might be safe until the robots come, three years later, but then that goes too. Gareth's joinery would last a bit longer, so we'd be living on one wage, and his isn't steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the packing side straight away if they'd have me. We'd have a small wedding at church with just family, and put the money towards rent. We'd probably move in with my parents to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like being told the floor is moving and nobody knows where.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for big schemes. Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to that, yes, I suppose. I'd feel I'd failed. I'd rather my dad helped first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first night look like when you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé and I would sit in the kitchen with the wedding folder open, crossing things out. And then praying, if I'm honest.

say: I'd say **families and churches** should pull together.
I'd say even **big government** help might be needed, uneasily.
think: I think my marketing job **goes within the year**, and packing three years later.
We'd live on **Gareth's joinery** wage, which isn't steady.
do: Move to the **packing side** straight away.
Have a **small church wedding** with family only.
Move in with **my parents** to save rent.
S2.quote: My fiancé and I would sit in the kitchen with the wedding folder open, crossing things out.
fieldNote: Her **traditional** instincts clash with needing state help in a crisis.
She sees the **packing line** as only a three-year refuge.
Faith and **family** are her first lines of support.

steps.text: Move to the jam company's packing line
Hold a small church wedding with family only
Move in with her parents to save on rent
Ask her dad for help before any government scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to get ready the old-fashioned way, by working and learning a trade. I'd say apprenticeships are better than handouts. I'd say that at church and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the marketing job, just not in a panic. Like with the fast one, the office goes first and the hands-on work later. Five years means I could learn something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at an apprenticeship in something hands-on that people want from a real person, maybe upholstery, which Gareth's trade sits next to. We could work together one day. We'd go ahead with the wedding, small, and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I could pray about and work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Upholstery robots would come around 2034 on this card. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. People buy our jams because they're made properly, and I'm hoping they'll pay for handmade furniture the same way. Maybe that's wishful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the AI tools? Would you try them in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe just the basics, to keep the job while I train. I'd still read everything printed out. I'm not going to change that.

say: I'd say five years is time to prepare by **learning a trade**.
I'd say **apprenticeships** beat handouts, at church and at home.
think: I think I'd still **lose the marketing job**, just not in a panic.
Five years means I could **learn something properly**.
do: Start an **upholstery apprenticeship**, next to Gareth's joinery.
Go ahead with a **small wedding** and keep saving.
Learn the **AI basics** only to keep the job while training.
feel: Worried, but it's a worry I could **pray about**.
S3.quote: People buy our jams because they're made properly, and I'm hoping they'll pay for handmade furniture the same way.
fieldNote: She bets on **handmade** goods, just like the jam brand's appeal.
She admits the **robot timeline** may catch upholstery too.
Her plan ties her work to her fiancé's **joinery**.

steps.text: Start an upholstery apprenticeship alongside Gareth's joinery
Go ahead with a small, cheap wedding
Learn basic AI writing tools only to keep the job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so people should take responsibility and prepare. Families, firms and churches can do a lot in ten years. I'd still not be keen on the government taking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right in this one. I'd have time to get better at my job, have the wedding, maybe a baby, and then train in upholstery when it makes sense. I'd be thirty-seven, with years still ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the jam company, work hard and try to be less slow. We'd have the wedding as planned next autumn. In a few years I'd start upholstery evening classes and build up slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more hopeful. Ten years is long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan for children in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in three or four years. With the fast one, I'd be scared to. Ten years makes having a baby feel normal again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm slow at learning things, and ten years might still not be enough for someone like me. But at least I could try.

say: I'd say people should **take responsibility** and prepare.
I'd say **families, firms and churches** can do a lot in ten years.
think: I think I'd be **all right** in this one.
I'd have time for the **wedding**, maybe a baby, then a trade.
do: Stay at the **jam company** and work on being less slow.
Hold the **wedding** next autumn as planned.
Start **upholstery evening classes** in a few years.
S4.quote: Ten years makes having a baby feel normal again.
fieldNote: Ten years restores her **family plans**: wedding and children.
She worries she may be **too slow** even with time.
She still prefers **family and church** to government help.

steps.text: Keep working at the jam company and improve her writing
Hold the wedding next autumn and plan for a baby
Start upholstery evening classes in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. The wedding, the job and Gareth's work all wobbling at once. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people my age, paid, so I could learn a trade without leaning on anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people I know would get through this through church, not through apps or schemes. That matters more than people think.

headlineQuote: A lot of people I know would get through this through church, not through apps or schemes.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** junior at an eighty-year-old jam company, writing catalogues and gift cards.
She's saving for a **wedding** next autumn with Gareth, a joiner, on thin savings.
She never uses AI, blames **herself** rather than firms, and turns to family and church.
She goes from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and hopeful with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with the **wedding, job** and Gareth's work wobbling at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** so she can learn a trade without leaning on anyone.
